items.title: RFC: Support building bpftrace for Android/AArch64
items.body:
## Summary

The bpftrace mainline currently does not provide a supported Android build
environment. The known Android-related environment is:

https://github.com/facebookexperimental/ExtendedAndroidTools/tree/main

It depends on the Android NDK and requires additional adaptation. It cannot
be used as a drop-in build environment for the latest bpftrace mainline code.

This RFC proposes adding a separate, reproducible cross-build environment for
AArch64 bpftrace. It builds bpftrace and its user-space dependencies from
pinned source revisions and can produce a fully-static executable suitable
for deployment on an Android AArch64 device.

The proposal does not modify bpftrace or the source code of its dependencies.
It adds a build environment and deployment workflow around the existing
source trees.

## Motivation

An Android device may not provide compatible development packages or the
matching LLVM, Clang, libbpf, BCC, elfutils, libpcap, and other libraries
required by bpftrace. A dynamically linked binary therefore requires
additional target-side library packaging and compatibility work.

A fully-static executable avoids requiring those bpftrace-specific shared
libraries on the target. This provides a practical deployment path for
devices where building or installing the complete dependency set is not
possible.

## Proposed workflow

The prototype provides a one-command build:

    ./scripts/build-all.sh

It downloads pinned sources, builds the dependencies from source,
cross-compiles LLVM/Clang and bpftrace for AArch64, performs an ELF audit,
and creates a deployment archive suitable for `adb push`. All build steps
use `-j3`.

Cross-build-specific behavior is kept in external build scripts, an
external CMake dependency configuration, a static-link wrapper, and staging
scripts. The normal native bpftrace build remains unchanged.

## Source-code impact

The prototype does not modify:

  - bpftrace C++ source code or upstream CMake source files;
  - LLVM/Clang source code;
  - libbpf, BCC, elfutils, libpcap, blazesym, or other dependency source
    code.

The user-space dependencies are built from source. The final static binary
contains the required static archives, including `libelf.a`, and does not
require `libelf.so.1` or other bpftrace-specific shared libraries at runtime.

## Prototype and Android test

The prototype produces an AArch64 executable with no dynamic section,
interpreter, or `DT_NEEDED` entries. It has been substantially validated with
an Android AArch64 device.

The preliminary test was performed using:

    adb push staging/bpftrace-aarch64/bin/bpftrace /data/bpftrace
    adb shell chmod 755 /data/bpftrace
    adb shell /data/bpftrace --version
    adb shell /data/bpftrace --help
    adb shell "/data/bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched* { @[probe] = count(); } interval:s:5 { exit(); }'"
 Attached 37 probes
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_kthread_stop_ret]: 1
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_kthread_stop]: 2
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_wait_task]: 3
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_process_exec]: 7
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_prepare_exec]: 7
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_process_wait]: 15
@[tracepoint:sched:sched_pi_setprio]: 96

readelf -d bpftrace

There is no dynamic section in this file.


## Platform scope

The initial prototype uses an AArch64 GNU/Linux cross toolchain and evaluates
the resulting executable on Android. AArch64 GNU/Linux/glibc and Android
NDK/bionic are different targets and should not be treated as identical.
Official Android NDK/bionic support may require a separate toolchain
configuration.

## Questions

1. Is Android/AArch64 cross compilation a use case the bpftrace project wants
   to support?
2. Should this build environment live in the bpftrace repository or in a
   separate packaging/build repository?
3. Is a fully-static executable a useful supported deployment option?
4. Should Android NDK/bionic and AArch64 GNU/Linux/glibc be treated as
   separate targets?
5. Is an external build environment preferable to changes in bpftrace's
   upstream CMake configuration?

The prototype is intended to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach.
If the direction is acceptable, a follow-up proof-of-concept pull request can
provide implementation details, documentation, and tests linked to this RFC.

items.title: Not functioning! The kernel space memory watchpoint not working in arm64, debian 12 & ubuntu 20
Overhaul release assets
items.body:
Our current release assets are a bit messy. Take for example https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/releases/tag/v0.22.1. We upload:

* binary_tools_man-bundle.tar.xz
* binary_tools_man-bundle.tar.zst
* bpftrace
* man.tar.xz
* tools-with-help.tar.xz
* tools.tar.xz

The intent was to pre-package some popular combinations. That was nice for a time, but now we want to add aarch64 artifacts (https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/2868). In the future, possibly even more. If we are to continue with current scheme, we'd be unnecessarily multiplying number of artifacts.

Let's simplify. I propose:
* Remove combinations. Just let users pick and choose what they want.
  * It's also more flexible.
* Remove multiple compression options and stick to zstd.
  * Originally in 2021 zstd was not as popular so we mainly used xz, but 4 years later and the entire internet is standardizing around zstd.
* Suffix bpftrace binary with architecture

Under new scheme (with additional aarch64), the artifacts would be:
* bpftrace.x86-64
* bpftrace.aarch64
* man.tar.zst
* tools.tar.zst
* tools-help.tar.zst

Note the suffix change from `zstd` -> `zst`. `zst` is the extension as documented by [RFC 8878](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8878).

Also note we don't compress the appimage binaries. Appimage already does compression.

items.title: Add support to printf() for dynamic width and precision specification
items.body:
Currently printf() only supports modifier width and precision specifications that are static in the printf string, e.g:

```
sudo src/bpftrace -e 'BEGIN{printf("%10s %10.3s\n", "hello", "jello");}'
Attaching 1 probe...
     hello        jel
```

If we implement dynamic width and precision specifiers according to the C standard then we can do this dynamically with:

```
sudo src/bpftrace -e 'BEGIN{printf("%*s %*.*s\n", 10, "hello", 10, 3, "jello");}'
Attaching 1 probe...
     hello        jel
```

This is super helpful for adding manual flow indentation in scripts, for example. (related: #2683) . I have these changes 3/4 implemented.

items.title: usdt: How to know number of the args dynamically
items.body:
For USDT, there are builtin variables `arg0`, `arg1`, ..., `argN`. - Arguments to the traced function; assumed to be 64 bits wide.
But if we want to trace multiple USDTs together, and each of them has different number of argements, it is very difficult to write the bpftrace script.
We have to list each USDT seperatly but with duplicate entries, because we have no signal on how many arguements it actually has.
And `arg0`, `arg1`, ... are tested statically during compilation, so not possible to workaround it, e.g. save the number of arguements as `arg0`, then iterate `arg1`, `arg2` ... under the hint of `arg0`.

Sample:
```
TRACE0(TRACE, TEST0);
TRACE1(TRACE, TEST1, 1); 
```
```
usdt:xxx.TRACE.TEST0,
usdt.xxx.TRACE.TEST1
{
  printf("%d\n", arg0);    <- compile error: "couldn't get argument 0"
}
```

items.title: RFC: Optimizing standard library bpf.c files
items.body:
As more bpf.c files get added to the standard library each time bpftrace is invoked these files need to parsed, compiled, BTF extracted, and linked. This will start to have a negative affect on startup latency (though more testing/benchmarking is needed to find out how much).

There are (at least) two options, which aren't mutually exclusive:
- conditionally include bpf.c files based on static analysis of the program ([Example PR](https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/pull/4743))
- cache compilation of these bpf.c files ([Example PR](https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/pull/4749))

I'm personally in favor of starting with option 1 and adding caching as a next layer (as needed) but we want something that is less cumbersome than the option in the example PR (basically keeping a map of external function to bpf.c file). Perhaps adding a simple namespacing like syntax when calling external stdlib functions, e.g., `usdt::__usdt_arg(...)` which indicates we need to import `usdt.bpf.c` or `util/strings::__str_contains(...)` to import `util/strings.bpf.c`. Most (if not all) of these external stdlib bpf.c calls will be hidden from the user as they are wrapped in macros so they can be a little verbose.

Other ideas/suggestions are welcome. Mostly creating this issue as a tracking task.

items.title: btf: only load the module for source-location kprobes
items.body:
Follow-up to #5308, which is now merged.

### Fix
Source-location kprobes previously resolved FILE:LINE to an address without
specifying the owning kernel module.

This change records the owning module returned by the DWARF lookup in
 AttachPoint::target, so the module BTF lookup uses the module containing the
source location.

This confirms that only the owning module BTF is selected. Type resolution for
kernel kprobes is handled separately in #5346.

Closes #5329

items.title: Typedefs not handled
items.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Currently, including C headers which include typedefs are not handled properly by bpftrace; in some cases, it's possible to use them, but you have to add `struct` before them, and in other cases, the type itself simply isn't recognized. By "not recognized," I mean that `SemanticAnalyser::resolve_struct_type` throws an error.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Currently, it appears as if `ClangParser::visit_children` should simply handle the case where `clang_getCursorKind(c) == CXCursor_TypedefDecl`. If it sees a `typedef` for a particular struct, it should add it to the `structs` map, like all other structs. This seems to be the simplest way to fix this, but ignores other types that are `typedef`d.

### Describe alternative solutions or features you've considered

Properly keeping track of new types (apart from structs specifically) seems like the correct solution. We could have a new map of types, exactly like the `structs` map.

items.title: kprobe: Add suport for attaching kprobes via source location
items.body:
This commit introduces support of DWARF debuginfo parsing for kernel and its modules, enabling kprobes to be attached using source location, similiar to the uprobe variant introduced in (#4867)[https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/pull/4867].

If the necessary DWARF files are availabile (`vmlinux` for running kernel, `*.ko`/`*.ko.zst` for loaded modules), kprobes can be attached via the `kprobe@FILE:LINE[:COL]` syntax. Kernel modules must be loaded prior to attachment, as DWARF information is only parsed for currently loaded modules.

Examples:

```
kprobe@br.c:29 {...}
kprobe@fs/vfs_open:1077 {...}
```

items.title: CMake: Fix circular static library dependencies
items.body:
Stacked PRs:
 * #5167
 * __->__#5166


--- --- ---

### CMake: Fix circular static library dependencies


Some internal static libraries may have subtle circular dependencies.
In particular:
- attachpoint_passes.cpp uses Dwarf from dwarf_parser.cpp
- attachpoint_passes.cpp is in the `ast` target which is normally linked
  *after* the `runtime` target

This may lead to the following linker error:

    /usr/bin/ld.bfd: ast/libast.a(attachpoint_passes.cpp.o): [...]
    [...] undefined reference to `bpftrace::DwarfParseError::ID'

Fix the issue by wrapping the linked libraries with `--start-group` and
`--end-group`, which allows the linker to resolve the dependencies
properly.

Signed-off-by: Viktor Malik <viktor.malik@gmail.com>

items.title: Proposal: namespaces and import resolution
items.body:
This is a sub-proposal for #3773. It is intended to hash out namespaces per the [comment](https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/pull/3781#issuecomment-2662978463) on the POC.

First, some basic requirements for namespaces:
* Provide a simple mechanism to avoid ambiguity as programs get larger.
* Provide a way to clearly distinguish external types and maps from internal types, if desired.

And some anti-requirements:
* Don't add significant complexity or cognitive overhead.
* Be familiar to users of namespaces in other languages (e.g. C++), but don't over-index on these.

# Basics

For simplicity, I propose no explicit `namespace` keywords or `using` keywords. The namespace for an identifier is specified using C++ syntax. This is to avoid ambiguity for field access. For example, an identifier `foo` in the `std` namespace can be specified as `std::foo`.

Namespaces are defined implicitly based on the script or import **directory**. The directory is chosen to allow users the flexibility of not using namespaces, or easily combining multiple separate objects into a single namespace, or adding directory structure to avoid ambiguity. For external, a user may prefer to add their external BPF programs into an `extern` directory, and then `import "extern/thing1"` or `import "extern/thing2"` as needed. Or they may prefer to simply ship their script and external object together, and `import "thing1"`.

Imports will be resolved using two paths:
* First, the directory that contains the script itself will be checked. Only directories that are not world-writable will be walked.
* Second, bpftrace may have embedded file contents that match the given import paths.

Additional paths can be added via a command-line option or via an environment variable.

Namespaces apply to all objects that may be imported: external maps, functions, and macros.

## Default namespace

The `bpftrace` script always lives in the "default" namespace, which is effectively the empty string. Therefore `foo` and `::foo` are equivalent. While this may seem insignificant, it is a useful mechanism to resolve ambiguity. User types for each probe will be prioritized when resolving types. These are not namespaced, and therefore `foo` can resolve to a user type, while `::foo` will resolve to the `bpftrace` type.

The standard library also lives in the "default" namespace. By default, a special module named `builtins` will be imported (unless a `--nostdlib` option is provided). Since `builtins` does not have a directory component, there is no special handling; this be imported into the default namespace. Over time, this import may contain other imports and macros to wrap calls to other namespaces, etc.

## Other namespaces

As noted above, namespaces are strictly a result of the **directory** that a given import lives in.

Consider the following:
```
import "foo"
import "bar/foo"
```

This will process two imports, and one will be available in the "default" namespace, and the next will be available in the `bar` namespace.

Import statements are always absolute, and will always resolve given the order above. This eliminates some classes of ambiguity regarding the structure (did you mean subdirectory foo? Or top-level module foo?). It also ensures that namespaces are used consistently, even within imported code. `bar::baz` always means the same thing, regardless of where it is called from.

Note that namespaces are also nested. Consider the following:
```
import "bar/baz/foo"
```

This imports into the `bar::baz` namespace, and would therefore require calls like `bar::baz::foo`. Note that within the implementation, this namespace will be mangled as "bar/baz", but the syntax must use `::` separators, not directory separators.

items.title: RFC: ustack() with eh_frame information
items.body:
Currently, user mode stack walking (ustack()) relies on frame pointers to be present, which is rarely the case. So ustack() in its current state often produces incomplete stacks.
There are a few tickets related to this:
* https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/1006
* https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/1744
* https://github.com/iovisor/bcc/issues/1234

A possible solution would be to parse the eh_frame/debug_frame sections of the binary and all loaded libs, convert them to tables and push as maps to an eBPF program that does the stack walking.
The tables can be kept pretty compact without sacrificing direkt access to each row, as opposed to walking the full function as in dwarf.
This approach also makes it possible to restore the registers at each frame, giving access to the function arguments. This should be optional, as it comes with a higher runtime cost during stack walking.

This has been done before, for example here
https://www.polarsignals.com/blog/posts/2022/11/29/dwarf-based-stack-walking-using-ebpf
Although they don't restore all registers.

A different solution would be to just copy the user stack and do the walking in user space, as danobi suggested here
https://dxuuu.xyz/stack-symbolize.html. As user stacks can grow pretty large, this approach imho is not feasible for high frequency probes. It also eliminates the possibility to further process the stack inside the probe.

The kernel approach with ORC is also similar.

Upsides:
 * proper stack frames in most environments
 * stack frames with arguments possible

Downsides:
  If the user works in an environment with full frame pointers, using eh_frame information would slow down stack walking. So we should give the user the choice to solely rely on frame pointers.

Implementation:
My idea is to provide the table builder as a standalone library, along with some bpf code, so that it can be used by more than just bpftrace. To find the best way to integrate this into bpftrace I might need some advice/discussion.

The current status is that I have a prototype that works well as a standalone program.

items.title: RFC: Release targets

This is a fork off of the discussion from #342 @danobi 

The idea here is to use the existing CI build for bpftrace to generate various release targets when the release process is initiated by `git tag`. 

These artifacts should be attached to a Release object from the github API transparently. 

It may also make sense to use this process to drive publishing artifacts to other systems, such as:

- Publishing a debian package to an iovisor-hosted apt repo
- Publishing a flatpak or snapcraft image
- Pushing a docker image to quay.io/iovisor/bpftrace or dockerhub

I think that this wolud help to make bpftrace more accessible.

This issue mostly supposes that #1041 makes sense, and bits like authenticating with quay.io/iovisor images would help to speed up CI runs, which is itself a concern of #1041 

# Implementation

Most of this comes down to someone with credentials on the various package publishing system to encrypt them and store them in the travis.yml

Travis itself provides deploy hooks that are probably flexible enough to initiate almost any process.

Most of these artifacts already exist, and deploy steps just need to be configured to copy them or do some packaging post-processing.

# Side benefit - Faster CI builds

If we can get access to push images from previous runs, we only rebuild layers when necessary. Each build type can have their own docker tag based on their ENV vars. This could help drop CI times significantly, depending on the docker pull speed.

items.title: Proposal: extensibility and interop
items.body:
> NOTE: this proposal is inspired and informed heavily by #3610. This is a large over-arching proposal, which will require multiple sub-proposals and implementation steps. This lays out the high-level concept and some of the details, but is not intended to be a complete answer to every future question.

Currently, bpftrace suffers from a few challenges:

* Advanced use cases can quickly hit barriers in terms of functionality. 
* Development velocity is slow due to the cross-cutting nature of changes, and the degree to which bespoke IR generation is required for most things.

In order to solve these problems, it will be useful to introduce the ability to dynamically extend the functionality of bpftrace by writing plain C, BPF C, or additional bpftrace scripts. Over time, internal functionality that is considered part of the “standard library” should migrate to these mechanisms, leaving only minimal core functionality where bespoke IR generation and plumbing is needed.

I propose adding a new statement, “import”:

```
import “dir/basename”
```

This statement will cause bpftrace to look for three different categories of extension. At least one of these must be present, and many cases will have more than one:
* A host file: `dir/basename.c`
  * Alternately, the user may provide `dirname/basename.so` to avoid compilation in the hot path. **This file must have BTF types attached already (e.g. pahole -J `dir/basename.so` when building).**
* A BPF file: `dir/basename.bpf.c`
  * Alternately, the user may provide `dirname/basename.bpf.bc` to avoid compilation in the hot path (but still allow full inlining)
  * Alternately, the user may provide `dirname/basename.bpf.o` to support arbitrary BPF programs (without inlining)
* A bpftrace file: `dir/basename.bt`

The host file can be used to provide dynamic user-space runtime behavior and types. The BPF can be used to provide bespoke BPF helper functions as well as pre-defined probes and maps. The bpftrace file can be used to provide user-defined bpftrace functions, as well as import additional modules. Each of these mechanisms is described in depth below.

Explicitly this proposal has no namespaces for imported extensions. This is to avoid the complexity (which is typically needed only for large-scale code bases) and more easily enable core extensions and internal types/functions to shift to using this model.

In the future, extensions can also be found in an archive file, e.g. `foo.zip`, which would be evaluated as though it was available in the local source directory. This simplifies distribution.

The details of each of these is described here, followed by a proposed implementation.

# Overview

When the import statement is found, the imported module will be evaluated (recursively, so leafs are ultimately instantiated first – cycles are not allowed).

For the bpftrace files, these are evaluated and loaded into the ASTContext. For example, configuration blocks are appended recursively in a depth-first manner, as are subprograms and probes. There is no specific intermediate format for compiled extensions. (If needed, you can distribute extensions as a `.zip` file, and use the `.so` and `.bpf.bc` formats described below to avoid higher costs for loaded extensions.)

For host field and BPF files, these are generally handled as:
* If a source file is available:
  * An in-memory version of the source file is generated which also contains necessary suitable BTF-generated type definitions for all currently known types (from the host layer or the BPF layer).
  * Common & necessary headers are automatically made available from embedded versions to eliminate the need for any system headers (e.g. vendored bpf.h). This allows the extensions to be built using e.g. `BPF_CORE_READ` and suitable annotations are injected.
* If either the source was generated above, or the serialized bytecode was available, then the source is compiled or the bytecode deserialized. This is all done with the existing embedded libclang. This module can be queried and either:
    * Modified and linked (Linker.linkModuleIn) into the current llvm.Module (for the BPF code).
    * Modified and compiled to either a shared object or as part of the emitted AOT binary. The shared object is subsequently loaded dynamically via `dlopen` and symbols found via `dlsym`.
* Type information and function information is extracted (either from the `llvm.Module` or via the embedded BTF in the binary) and used internally for compiling the bpftrace program.
* After the bpftrace program has been compiled and code generated, the associated `llvm::Module`s for the imported extensions are appropriately linked (as a dynamic object, or in the LLVM-sense for the BPF code) to the current module.

# Existing maps and probes

When the `.bpf.c` source file is first transformed into an `llvm::Module` we will scan for all global variables in a `.maps` section and suitably register these as `@name` values usable by all probes. This can also be done with a binary file via the BTF information. (It is not clear whether we will always convert to BTF first, but the same concept applies either way.) This is the “escape hatch” that can be used to define individual maps with whatever types you like – using the BPF C syntax. These variables will be linked in at the end and usable by the generated programs.

Similarly, existing probes are scanned by looking at standard BPF section names. During attach time, these probes will be attached to the noted attach points.

# The standard library

Eventually, we can embed a set of files for a standard library within bpftrace that are parsed and loaded through this extension mechanism. For example, consider: `std/core.c`, `std/core.bpf.c` and `std/core.bt` files and an implicit `import “std/core”` in every program. These could be broken up into different components (and `std/core.bt` could load those), or parts of the standard library could be optional and loaded manually (e.g. `import “std/python”`).

Over time many of the internal types and details can be moved to a combination of bpftrace user-defined functions, native BPF code, and C helper code. This relies on the asynchronous function extensibility and type extensibility describe below, each of which will require richer proposals.

# Asynchronous functions

> This will be refined and implemented as part of a later proposal. This is a sketch for how this will relate to the extensions.

All exported (non-static) functions in the host file are selected. These are new asynchronous function targets. bpftrace assigns each of these functions a unique identifier for dispatch and adds the functions to a large dispatch table (this dispatch table must be serialized for the AOT case). Note that the names for these functions are suitably mangled such that they are resolvable in the standard way during AST passes and analysis.

When reloading the final linked shared object, each of these symbols is resolved within the dispatch table. (It is fine to use `dlsym` even if the symbol is in the main binary.) A final transformation pass is applied to the BPF code (at the LLVM level, since it must include extern IR as well) that transforms a call to a function of this name to the bytecode that pushes the asynchronous call to the ring buffer.

# Types

> This will be refined and implemented as part of a later proposal. This is a sketch for how this will relate to the extensions.

In reality, types in bpftrace exist in two different worlds (BPF and userspace) and need not be exactly the same. The use of types is technically isolated within each extension, e.g. a `foo.c` file may define a `struct foo` and use it freely within its own functions. The complexity arises when the functions in the BPF world would like to pass these types to the user space helpers (which at least is a one-way transformation).

Custom types can be defined by the existence of a function named `serialize_` in the BPF source file, and functions prefixed `deserialize_`, `free_` (*), `emit_raw_` and `emit_json_` in the C source file with the same name. These functions will be automatically called to serialize and deserialize these types when making asynchronous calls (e.g. as part of the IR generated with the call replacement noted above), and will be used to back the `print` implementation.

(*) The `free_` method will be called with the returned value (register only) when the value is discarded. This allows dynamic memory management to be used for the serialized types, supporting e.g. proper strings in userspace.

The named types that can be used in probes are defined from the types defined in the BPF extensions. For example, a kernel probe will have `builtin + stdlib + custom_includes + extensions+ vmlinux` types available. A module would have `builtin + stdlib + custom_includes + extensions+ vmlinux + module` types. A user probe would have `builtin + stdlib + custom_includes + extensions + types_from_debuginfo` available. Currently, all probes have the same set of types available, and refining this to be a union over a specific set is a future proposal.

# Implementation steps (sketch)

General structure:
* For module loading:
  * If `.bpf.c` is available and is not older than a `.bpf.bc` module, then compile that to LLVM bytecode.
    * If LLVM bytecode is available and is not older than a `.bpf.o`, then compile the bytecode to an object.
    * Pull BTF information from the `bpf.o`, which must always be available if any of the above are available.
  * For final compilation:
    * If LLVM bytecode is available, inline all functions and link them into module.
    * Otherwise, probes are loaded and linked as BPF objects directly from the object file.
 * Start with the simplest case: import “.o” and load existing maps and tracepoints.
* Next, proceed to support additional cases and refine iteratively.

items.title: Macros: Add support for typeof args
items.body:
Stacked PRs:
 * __->__#5234


--- --- ---

### Macros: Add support for typeof args


This allows us to do type expression substitution in bpftrace macros.
For example:
```
macro sof_double(type_a, type_b) {
  sizeof(type_a) + sizeof(type_b[2])
}

begin {
  print(sof_double(typeof(struct qspinlock), typeof(uint64*)));
}
```
Expands to:
```
begin {
  print(sizeof(struct qspinlock) + sizeof(uint64*[2]));
}
```

This is only valid for macros so if a call signature doesn't match a macro
then a compile time error is issued as `typeof` is not a valid expression.

This wrapping of type expressions in `typeof` is neccessary to prevent a
parsing ambiguity, e.g. `x[2]`. Without a wrapping `typeof` we don't know
if this is an array access or an array of two `x` elements. Inside of a
`typeof` it's always parsed as the latter.

items.title: ClangParser: fix --include for kernel and C standard headers
items.body:
Fixes #3473.

## Problem

When BTF is enabled, `ClangParser` defines `_LINUX_TYPES_H` so kernel types can
come from BTF. At the same time, `/bpftrace/include` was passed as an
`-isystem` directory. Clang could therefore select an incomplete system
`linux/types.h` instead of bpftrace's UAPI-compatible copy, leading to missing
types such as `__aligned_u64` when a user supplied kernel or transitive system
header.

Prioritizing `/bpftrace/include` exposed two related C-header problems:

- bpftrace's embedded `stdint.h` and `limits.h` reused Clang's
  `__CLANG_*` include guards. Their `#include_next` entered Clang's copy after
  already defining the same guard, so Clang skipped its header and types or
  macros disappeared.
- Standard macros such as `UINTPTR_MAX` contain valid uppercase integer
  suffixes such as `UL`, while `util::to_uint()` only accepted lowercase
  suffixes.

An earlier revision removed the embedded headers and added `clang-unwrapped`
to the Nix environment. Rechecking that approach showed that it created a
runtime dependency on compiler resource headers, still failed `limits.h` on
the LLVM 18–20 Nix jobs, and interfered with the Nix compiler wrapper in an
LLVM 22 Clang build.

## Solution

- Pass only `/bpftrace/include` as `-I`, ensuring that bpftrace's compatibility
  headers take precedence.
- Keep discovered system and architecture directories as `-isystem`.
- Retain the embedded `stdint.h` and `limits.h`, but give them
  bpftrace-specific include guards so `#include_next` can enter Clang's copy.
- Provide a `UINTPTR_MAX` spelling that also works with LLVM 18's detailed
  preprocessing record.
- Accept uppercase `U`/`L` C integer suffixes while leaving bpftrace time-unit
  suffixes case-sensitive.
- Try `clang-<LLVM major>` and then unversioned `clang` when discovering system
  include directories. Success is tracked independently for each attempt.
- Add parser and runtime coverage for the kernel-header path, standard-header
  macros, and environments where no Clang executable is available at runtime.

This keeps bpftrace usable in packaged or minimal environments without making
a Clang executable a mandatory runtime dependency.

## Verification

I first checked the rebased upstream revision without this patch:

- Debian Sid, LLVM 21: `linux/sched.h` parses on the current 6.12 kernel, but
  `UINTPTR_MAX` is unknown and `UINT_MAX` cannot be expanded.
- Fedora Rawhide, LLVM 22: the Infiniband reproduction still fails while
  parsing `infiniband/verbs.h`, with missing `uint8_t`, `uint32_t`, and
  `uint64_t`.

The updated patch was then tested as follows:

| Environment | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Nix, LLVM 18.1.8 | Build passes; `stdint.h` and `limits.h` pass with normal `PATH` and `PATH=/nonexistent` |
| Debian Sid, LLVM 21.1.8 | Focused runtime suite passes 5/5 |
| Fedora Rawhide, LLVM 22.1.8 | `linux/sched.h`, `stdint.h`, `limits.h`, and `infiniband/verbs.h` pass with normal `PATH` and `PATH=/nonexistent` |
| Parser/Clang unit coverage | New uppercase-suffix tests and all Clang parser tests pass |
| Formatting | `git clang-format --diff upstream/master` reports no changes; `git diff --check` passes |

The full local unit run passed 979/980 tests. The only failure was
`pid_filter_pass.no_add_filter`, which is unrelated to the changed files and
passed twice when rerun independently.

The previously requested `tests/codegen-tests.sh` command exits successfully.
Upstream removed the codegen test suite in November 2025, so the script now
only reports that those tests are deprecated and no longer exist.

The exact Debian 10/custom 5.4 kernel environment from #3473 was not recreated.
The later Infiniband reproduction documented on this PR was reproduced against
current upstream and passes with this patch.

items.title: Don't error on integer sign mismatch
items.body:
Stacked PRs:
 * #5152
 * __->__#5148


--- --- ---

### Don't error on integer sign mismatch


This error has been a constant source of pain for users and is not worth
the possible prevention of strange behavior.

Instead replace errors with a simple warning when we create an implicit
cast that may cause truncation, reinterpretation, or undefined behavior.

The general idea here is that we don't want bpftrace to get in the way of
its users. Many dynamically typed languages (e.g. Python and Javascript)
don't even support unsigned integers because of the problems they cause.

This will also remove the pain of a recent breaking change to update the
types of integer literals and subtraction/decrement operations:
https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/pull/5138

This is an example that was previously invalid:
```
$a = (uint64)1;
$a = (int64)2;
```
Now the resulting type of `$a` is an int64 and an implicit cast (with a
warning) is inserted at the first assignment: `$a = (int64)(uint64)1;`.

This will happen for map values/keys, scratch variables, and binops.
It is also applied to integers nested in tuples and records.

The behavior for flexible_sign types or positive integer literals is not
changed.

Additionally, there is no longer an error for variable declarations:
```
$b = -1;
let $a: uint16 = $b;
```
A cast will be inserted in front of `$b` to `uint16` and a warning will
occur.

However! If we can easily prove statically that an integer literal can not
fit into a specific type then there is an error. For example these are
errors:
```
let $a: uint16 = -1;
let $b: uint8 = 1000000000000;
$x = -1;
$x = 10223372036854775807;
```

As usual, warnings can be silenced with the `--no-warnings` flag.

When building with some C++ compilers, such as GCC 11 (and probably earlier versions), the static_assert(false, ...) in an else branch of a template in tests/async_action.cpp triggers the assertion and fails to compile even if T is one of the accepted types (string or integer).

items.title: Fix ASTSource line collection bug
items.body:
When collecting lines for an ASTSource object we use std::getline which skips the final empty line in a bpftrace script. This is problematic because for a script ending in a trailing new line the lexer advances line counter and the END token gets assigned this new line.

This becomes a real problem only in the case when we try to access this last line which happens when we set a warning (`addWarning`) or an error on the entire program node, which we do in the CreateClangBuildPass when there are clang warnings.

The access happens in location.cpp:
```
for (int i = begin.line; i <= end.line; i++) {
  assert(i <= static_cast<int>(source_->lines_.size()));
  result.push_back(source_->lines_[i - 1]);
}
```
As you can see there is an assert but these get stripped out in release builds.

The fix is to check if there is a trailing new line context.cpp when constructing the ASTSource object and emplace an empty new line into `lines_`.

Fixes: https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/5073

### Refactor TypeResolver pass


This replaces the current type_resolver with an entirely new architecture
for resolving types. It utilizes a constraint solver pattern for resolving
types in a graph.

More details on how all this works in the added readme:
docs/type_resolution.md

There are a few minor things to note:
- For maps where we can't infer the type, presume they are Int64. This is
  for cases where scripts have just `@a++` or `@a += 1` and no other assignment.
  It also means this is ok and prints `0`: `begin { $a = @a; print($a); }`.
- No longer preserve the original ordering of a variable, map key/value, if
  it's a record type. This was probably not working completely in trunk
  anyway but is more visible with how the TypeGraph resolves types.

This fixes this issue:
- https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/4926

There will be follow-up refactoring for both TypeChecker and it's suite of
unit tests. TypeChecker will be moved as another visitor inside of
CreateTypeResolverPass but it left out of this PR for simplicity and
verification that the end behavior hasn't changed.

items.title: Fix #4767: Add semantic analysis error for while loops with map variables in condition
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes issue #4767 where while loops using map variables in their condition were being rejected by the BPF verifier as infinite loops, causing confusing runtime errors.

## Problem

The BPF verifier cannot statically prove that loops are bounded when the condition depends on map variables (`@var`) because:
- Map variables can be modified by other programs or threads
- The verifier cannot track all possible modifications to map values
- This results in cryptic "infinite loop detected" errors at BPF load time

Example that was failing:
```bash
begin { @a = 0; while (@a < 1024) { print(1); ++@a; } }
```

Solution
This PR adds semantic analysis to detect this pattern early and provide clear guidance:

Early Detection: Added [MapVariableDetector](vscode-file://vscode-app/snap/code/211/usr/share/code/resources/app/out/vs/code/electron-browser/workbench/workbench.html) class using the Visitor pattern to identify map variable usage in while loop conditions
Clear Error Message: Provides actionable feedback suggesting the use of local variables instead
Comprehensive Coverage: Detects both simple map variables (@var) and map access expressions (@["key"])

items.title: Fix interval probe attachment when CPU 0 is offline (#4966)
items.body:
This PR addresses the issue where attaching `interval` probes fails when CPU 0 is offline (or hot-unplugged).

Previously, `AttachedIntervalProbe::make` hardcoded `cpu=0` when creating the perf event. This caused [open_perf_event](cci:1://file:///data/8797/nhlos/lagvm/LINUX/android/external/bpftrace/src/attached_probe.cpp:856:0-884:1) to fail if CPU 0 was not available.

This change updates it to utilize `util::get_online_cpus()` to dynamically select the first available online CPU, ensuring the probe can be attached successfully regardless of CPU 0's status. All other online CPUs are then looped over correctly as before.

Fixes #4966.

items.title: Add libbpf as a submodule
items.body:
Since #4264, we require linking against libbpf statically. Currently, we link against system libbpf but that brings all kinds of issues such as #4454 or #4429.

Additionally, bpftrace usually depends on a very recent, often unreleased, version of libbpf. To make the relationship between the two tighter, it makes sense to make libbpf a submodule of bpftrace and integrate libbpf build into our build process.

items.title: Consolidate linking of libbpf and bcc
items.body:
In CMake, we link `LIBBPF_LIBRARIES` and `LIBBCC_LIBRARIES` from several places, many of which are redundant. In addition, in one place, we link against `libbpf.a`, which CMake turns into `-Wl,-Bstatic -lbpf`, which causes system libbpf be used even if different `libbpf.a` was found in `FindBpf.cmake` (see #4454 for details).
    
Consolidate `CMakeLists.txt` files such that every target which needs `LIBBPF_LIBRARIES` and `LIBBCC_LIBRARIES` links them exactly once. Also drop linking libbpf from the `ast` target (which doesn't need it) and instead add it to the `util` target (since `util/bpf_progs.cpp` uses it).
    
To prevent the bug fixed by #4429 from repeating, add an explicit `-Wl,-Bstatic` before each linking of `libbpf.a`.

Finally, add a new section to `INSTALL.md` on how to build and install libbpf from source and how to point CMake to it when it is installed in a non-standard directory. This is useful especially since we now require the latest static libbpf library which many distros do not ship (they either shop too old libbpf or they don't ship static libraries).

This should resolve #4454.

items.title: macros: expand literals as literals
items.body:
Stacked PRs:
 * __->__#4418
 * #4417
 * #4401
 * #4416


--- --- ---

### macros: expand literals as literals


Currently we will assign literals to a temporary variable during
expansion. This may result in some type marshalling and an inability to
fold properly. This change allows literals to expand as literals, and
also ensures that they are not mutated (just like expressions
previously). Since they expand as literals, they will continue to be
folded during expansion.

In order to allow literals to be recursively folding, it was necessary
to pull folding ahead of expansion. The only problem with this is that
positional parameters are also folded. Therefore, we run a portability
check before and after parsing: first will capture positional
parameters, and afterwards will capture the use of any builtins, etc.
that may be non-portable.

With this in place, we can trivally support the creation of a
`static_assert` macro, which works as expected. It is mostly useful for
`sizeof`, `offsetof`, `typeof` and similar functions.

```
begin {
 static_assert(1 > 0, "the world is upside down");
 static_assert(1 < 0, "the world is okay");
}
```

Signed-off-by: Adin Scannell <amscanne@meta.com>

items.title: RFC: alternatives to static build
items.body:
During the BPF Microconference at LPC, we got feedback that installing llvm/clang/libbpfcc in production servers just to use `bpftrace` would be overkill and sometimes unfeasible. An alternative would be linking to those dependencies statically, but most distributions don't provide the static library `libclang.a` on their libclang packages.

I started to think about alternatives to a static build, and two ideas came up:

## Have an option to compile a `.bt` file into an executable

In this approach, we would add a new option to `bpftrace` (let's say, `-o`), which instead of attaching to the probes we provided, would build an executable binary with our bpftrace program. We could then send this binary to a given server without having to install llvm/clang libraries there.

Downsides would be:

  - bpftrace would get more complex
  - I think we would still need libbpfcc installed on the server to attach to probes

## Compile a `.bt` file into an intermediate format, and run with a minimal bpftrace binary

Similar to the previous idea, but instead of creating an executable binary we would have an intermediate format with our probes as well as BPF programs for each probe. We could then use a minimal bpftrace binary (not linked against llvm/clang) to run this intermediate file.

On the upside, I think this would be more maintainable than the previous approach (internally we could also use the intermediate format). Downsides are the same as the previous approach.

---

I still think it's worth getting our static builds to work though, but if we can't do that reliably, we could start investigating those alternatives.

items.title: build: remove `libbpf/bpf.h` and namespace guard
items.body:
Stacked PRs:
 * #4516
 * __->__#4513


--- --- ---

### build: remove `libbpf/bpf.h` and namespace guard


Since `libbpf` is a static dependency, it makes little sense to have a
manually curated vendored header as well.

Unfortunately, the use of this header is a bit of a mess. Since it
includes the lovely `#pragma once`, it will only be included once.
Unfortunately, our poor header hygiene means that in some places this
header was included in a namespace guard (e.g. putting all those types
into a `libbpf` namespace), and in other cases not.

One option might be to guard this header everywhere it is used, but
there are two major problems with this:

* This quickly becomes a pain if we actually do have IWYU hygiene, and
  include the header in files where these details are needed.

* Other libraries may need `libbpf` types, and putting them into a
  special namespace when we include them first breaks their use
  elsewhere. (Also applies to the case where these namespaced headers
  are including anything else. This is why it's a bad idea to have
  `#include` inside any namespace.)

The best approach here is to simply leave those types in the global
namespace (since it is a C library, after all), and try to introduce
sensible types and wrappers locally to minimize the need to exercise
that API surface. If we really want a `libbpf` namespace, then we should
do a proper C++ libbpf, rather than inconsistently loading that header
in a namespace.

Signed-off-by: Adin Scannell <amscanne@meta.com>

items.title: refactor: move to static types
items.body:
Stacked PRs:
 * #3998
 * #3997
 * __->__#3996


--- --- ---

### refactor: move to static types


This change makes AST node consistent, and adopts static types rather
than relying on RTTI.

The major motivation for this is to move away from the `Expression`
inheritence model, whereby instances reach into the `Expression` base
class and access the `SizedType` directly. Instead, a layer of
abstraction is added here to allow individual node to provide access to
their type information via a returned reference. Instead of being
specifically a `SizedType` object, this reference can be an abstract
type of some kind, e.g. originating outside of our own type system.

Consider a future pass which examines `Call` nodes, and replaces them
with `ExternalCall` nodes based on the resolve imports. The types for
those new `ExternalCall` nodes should be BTF types sourced from the
impored type information. Currently we would need to figure out a way to
convert every type exhaustively. While this is done currently within the
`BTF` class, it is all driven by the `ClangParser`. Reinvoking the
parser again and again in order to introduce these types to our unified
type universe is not ideal: we should be able to operate exclusively and
directly on the type information contained in the external objects. Over
time, our internal implementations will leverage these mechanisms,
allowing us to remove the special cases from `SizedType`.

With this change, individual node are still typed, but they have their
own field, appropriately named. Direct access to these fields are
encouraged, and this is where type inference will operate. This reduces
ambiguity, as node without fundamental type information (e.g. a
PositionalParameter, a Block, etc.) need not store an invalid value.
They can implement a `type` function which simply references to the
appropriate sub-type.

Note that the `type` method returns immutable references, which means
that type inference and code generation can only mutate types on node
that it understands, which is a desirable safety property. This is on
top of the additional safety properties that no more `static_cast`s or
`dynamic_cast`s are permitted, reducing the possibility of subtle memory
errors.

Most of this change itself is boilerplate in two forms:
* Making AST node consistent in structure and moving the `type`.
* Changing all call-sites to use this new consistent structure.

There should be no semantic change.

Signed-off-by: Adin Scannell <amscanne@meta.com>

items.title: Migrate usdt attachment from bcc to libbpf API
items.body:
`AttachedProbe::attach_usdt()` uses bcc's `bpf_attach_uprobe()` to attach usdt probes (which are actually just backed by uprobes). This can be migrated to libbpf's `bpf_program__attach_uprobe()`.

Note that `attach_usdt()` makes use of a few other bcc APIs. This issue does not intend to migrate those usages to libbpf ones. That task would be much harder. It should be doable, though. We'll eventually do it, but sooner is better than later. Many bonus points if you can figure that out. This might need to be done in sync with other parts of the codebase like codegen.
